lessons.title: The human reproductive systems and fertilisation
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Biology — Human reproduction, menstrual cycle, pregnancy, STIs and HIV (to be checked against the official syllabus; for health review)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name the parts of the male and female reproductive systems and their functions.
Describe the structure of sperm and egg cells.
reviewNotes: Content is anatomical and factual; to be reviewed by a health worker/teacher for age-appropriateness.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Male reproductive system
blocks.md:
- **Testes** (in the scrotum, slightly cooler than the body): make **sperm** and the hormone **testosterone**.
- **Sperm duct**: carries sperm to the urethra; **glands** (including the prostate) add fluid to form **semen**.
- **Urethra** inside the **penis**: carries semen (and urine, never at the same time) out of the body.

blocks.title: Female reproductive system
blocks.md:
- **Ovaries**: make **egg cells (ova)** and the hormones **oestrogen** and **progesterone**.
- **Oviducts** (fallopian tubes): carry eggs to the uterus; **fertilisation** takes place here.
- **Uterus** (womb): lining receives the embryo; **cervix**: ring of muscle at the base of the uterus; **vagina**: receives semen.

blocks.caption: Female reproductive system (schematic, front view).
blocks.alt: A pear-shaped uterus with two oviducts reaching to round ovaries, a short cervix below and the vagina leading out.

blocks.title: Gametes
blocks.md:
- **Sperm**: small, with a **tail** to swim, a head containing the nucleus and an **acrosome** with enzymes that digest the egg's coat, and many **mitochondria** for energy.
- **Egg**: much larger, contains a food store (yolk-like cytoplasm), a jelly layer and the nucleus; it cannot move by itself.

Both contain half the normal number of chromosomes (23).

blocks.title: Fertilisation and implantation
blocks.md: **Fertilisation** is the fusion of the nucleus of a sperm with the nucleus of an egg to form a **zygote** (46 chromosomes) in the oviduct. The zygote divides repeatedly to form a ball of cells (**embryo**) that moves to the uterus. **Implantation** is the sinking of the embryo into the thick uterus lining.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- The urethra carries both urine and semen in males, but not at the same time.
- Fertilisation happens in the oviduct, not the uterus.
- The sex of the baby depends on the sperm: X gives a girl, Y a boy (see genetics).

blocks.title: Fertilised egg chromosomes
blocks.statement: A human sperm cell has 23 chromosomes and an egg has 23. How many chromosomes does the zygote have and why?
steps: Each gamete has half the full number.
At fertilisation the two nuclei fuse: 23 + 23 = 46.

blocks.title: Where does it happen?
blocks.statement: Name the place where (a) eggs are made, (b) fertilisation occurs, (c) the embryo develops.
steps: (a) Eggs are made in the ovaries.
(c) The embryo implants and develops in the uterus.

blocks.title: Menstrual cycle
blocks.md: The **menstrual cycle** is a cycle of about **28 days** (it varies between women). Around **day 14** an egg is released from an ovary: **ovulation**. The uterus lining thickens in preparation for an embryo. If no embryo implants, the lining breaks down and leaves the body through the vagina in the **period** (menstruation, about days 1-5).

blocks.caption: A 28-day cycle (average).
blocks.alt: A bar over 28 days: a pink period of about days 1 to 5, an orange phase when the lining rebuilds to day 14 with an arrow marking ovulation, and a yellow phase when the lining is maintained until day 28.

blocks.title: Hormones and pregnancy
blocks.md: **Oestrogen** (from the ovary) helps rebuild the lining and triggers ovulation; **progesterone** maintains the lining. If the egg is fertilised and implants, progesterone stays high, the lining is kept and the periods stop. A missed period can be an early sign of pregnancy.

blocks.caption: A baby in the uterus (schematic).
blocks.alt: A uterus containing a baby surrounded by amniotic fluid, joined by an umbilical cord to the placenta on the uterus wall.

blocks.title: Placenta, birth and care
blocks.md:
The **placenta** brings the mother's and baby's blood very close so that **oxygen, glucose, amino acids and antibodies** pass to the baby and **carbon dioxide and urea** pass to the mother. The two bloods do **not** mix. The **umbilical cord** joins baby to placenta. **Amniotic fluid** protects the baby from knocks.

Pregnancy lasts about **40 weeks**. At birth the uterus muscles contract (labour), the cervix widens and the baby is born.

blocks.title: Antenatal care and breast-feeding (flag for health review)
blocks.md: Pregnant women should visit a clinic regularly, eat a balanced diet and avoid smoking, alcohol and untested medicines, which can harm the baby. **Breast milk** contains the right nutrients and **antibodies**; health services recommend exclusive breast-feeding for the first six months. HIV-positive mothers should follow the advice of their health worker.

blocks.title: Fertile days
blocks.statement: A cycle is 28 days long and ovulation occurs on day 14. If a period started on 1 March, on which date does ovulation occur, and when does the next period start?
steps: Day 14 counted from 1 March (day 1) is 14 March.
The next period starts on day 29, which is 29 March (1 March + 28 days).
blocks.answer: Ovulation about 14 March; next period about 29 March.

blocks.title: Why the blood does not mix
blocks.statement: Explain why it is important that the blood of the mother and the baby do not mix.
steps: The mother's blood pressure is too high for the baby's delicate capillaries, and the blood groups of mother and baby may differ.
Exchange occurs by diffusion and active transport across thin walls instead.
blocks.answer: Exchange across thin walls protects the baby without mixing the bloods.

blocks.title: STIs
blocks.md: **Sexually transmitted infections** are diseases passed from one person to another during unprotected sexual contact. Examples: **gonorrhoea** and **syphilis** (caused by bacteria and treated with antibiotics) and **HIV** (a virus). Some STIs show no signs, so people can pass them on without knowing.

blocks.caption: Types of STI and prevention.
blocks.alt: Three coloured boxes: bacterial STIs treated with antibiotics, viral STIs including HIV without a simple cure, and prevention by abstinence, faithfulness, condoms and testing.

blocks.title: HIV and AIDS
blocks.md:
**HIV** (human immunodeficiency virus) infects and destroys **lymphocytes** (white blood cells), so the immune system becomes weak. Without treatment, a person may develop **AIDS**: they get many infections that a healthy body would fight off.

**HIV is spread by**: unprotected sex; infected blood (shared needles or razors, unscreened blood); from an infected mother to her baby during pregnancy, birth or breast-feeding.

blocks.title: How HIV is NOT spread
blocks.md: HIV is **not** spread by hugging, shaking hands, sharing plates, cups or toilets, coughing, or **mosquito bites**. People living with HIV deserve respect and care. **Stigma** and discrimination discourage people from being tested and treated.

blocks.title: Prevention and treatment
blocks.md:
- **Abstinence** from sex until adulthood, and **faithfulness** to one uninfected partner.
- Correct and consistent use of **condoms** reduces the risk.
- Never share needles, razors or blades; blood for transfusion is screened.
- **Testing** and early treatment: **antiretroviral drugs** (ART) keep the virus under control, allow a long healthy life and greatly reduce passing the virus to others or to a baby; they are **not a cure**. Treatment is available at health centres.

blocks.title: True or false
blocks.statement: Decide whether HIV can pass between two friends who (a) share a plate of ndolé, (b) share a razor blade.
steps: (a) Sharing food or plates does not transmit HIV.
(b) Razors or blades can carry blood: sharing them can spread HIV if one person is infected.
blocks.answer: (a) No risk; (b) risk, so never share.

blocks.title: Mother and baby
blocks.statement: A pregnant woman learns she is HIV-positive. Name two actions that can protect her baby.
steps: She should attend antenatal clinics and take antiretroviral treatment as prescribed.
She should follow the health worker's advice on delivery and feeding the baby.
blocks.answer: Take ART and follow clinic advice for birth and feeding.
